title: How the US handed China control of the rare earth supply chain
gist: China controls roughly 60% of rare earth mining and 91% of separation/refining, giving it geopolitical leverage it demonstrated via 2025 export controls now suspended until November 10, 2026; the US has committed over $7 billion since April 2025 to rebuild domestic capacity (including a 15% Pentagon stake in MP Materials), but rebuilding a full mine-to-magnet supply chain is estimated to take up to 15 years and China has since sanctioned the two furthest-along US rare earth firms.

themes.theme: China's dominance and how it arose

insights.claim: China mined about 60 percent of the world's rare earth elements used in magnets in 2024 but handled about 91 percent of global separation and refining, giving it outsized control over the processing bottleneck rather than just raw extraction.
insights.speaker: The Conversation
insights.so_what: The 91% refining share (versus 60% mining share) is the key structural chokepoint: even non-Chinese mined rare earths largely must flow through Chinese processing, meaning diversifying mining alone won't reduce dependency without parallel refining capacity.
insights.locator: China, which mined about 60 percent of the world’s rare earth elements

insights.claim: California's Mountain Pass mine led world rare earth production until the late 1980s, but radioactive wastewater spills into the Mojave Desert made domestic production politically difficult; the separation plant closed in 1998 and the mine itself stopped in 2002 as China's cheaper processed materials made switching suppliers an easy economic decision.
insights.speaker: The Conversation
insights.so_what: Explains the historical mechanism (environmental liability plus lower Chinese costs) by which the US ceded rare earth leadership, a cautionary case study for other Western critical-minerals reshoring efforts facing similar environmental/cost tradeoffs.
insights.locator: Multiple instances of radioactive wastewater spilling

insights.claim: The US still imported more than two-thirds of the rare earth elements it used as recently as 2025, despite MP Materials restarting mining at Mountain Pass in 2017.
insights.speaker: The Conversation
insights.so_what: Shows that even years after reshoring efforts began, US import dependency remains structurally high (over two-thirds), underscoring how difficult and slow supply-chain reshoring is in practice.
insights.locator: MP Materials restarted mining there in 2017

insights.claim: Buyers who used Chinese processing got materials below the cost of producing them domestically and avoided environmental cleanup costs and bad press, but in exchange ceded strategic leverage to the processor — a tradeoff described as understood but underestimated while China was still considered a rising rather than dominant power.
insights.speaker: The Conversation
insights.so_what: Frames a general mental model applicable beyond rare earths: outsourcing strategically critical processing for short-term cost savings creates long-term geopolitical leverage risk, relevant to evaluating other critical-supply-chain dependencies (e.g., semiconductors, batteries).
insights.quote: They ceded leverage to the processor in exchange. The trade was understood.
insights.locator: Buyers using processing in China got material below

insights.claim: On October 9, 2025, China's Ministry of Commerce announced six wide-ranging export control measures, including Announcement No. 61, which requires a Chinese license for any product exported from any country if Chinese-origin rare earths make up 0.1 percent or more of its value, or if it uses Chinese rare earth technology.
insights.speaker: The Conversation
insights.so_what: A 0.1% value threshold extraterritorial licensing rule effectively gives China veto power over a vast range of global manufactured goods (electronics, autos, defense equipment) made anywhere in the world, a far more expansive form of leverage than simple export bans.
insights.locator: One, Announcement No. 61, affects what even factories abroad can export

insights.claim: After Trump met Xi Jinping in October 2025, Beijing suspended six export controls until November 10, 2026, in exchange for Washington pausing its 'affiliates rule' (restrictions on companies majority-owned by blacklisted firms) for one year; both suspensions snap back into place automatically unless both governments extend them.
insights.speaker: The Conversation
insights.so_what: November 10, 2026 is a concrete, trackable date on which a major trade truce could unwind automatically absent renewed negotiation, a clear catalyst date for markets exposed to rare-earth-dependent sectors (autos, defense, electronics).
insights.locator: After President Donald Trump met Chinese leader Xi Jinping

insights.claim: Licensing rules imposed by China in April 2025 on exports of seven heavier rare earths were never suspended and remain in effect regardless of the broader truce.
insights.speaker: The Conversation
insights.so_what: Even during the current 'truce' period, a subset of critical heavy rare earth exports remains restricted, meaning supply risk for downstream industries has not actually been fully resolved despite headline de-escalation.
insights.locator: Some of the export rules were never suspended

insights.claim: On June 22, 2026, China's Ministry of Commerce placed 10 US companies — mostly makers of drones, radar, aerospace systems, and military vehicles — on its export control list, barring Chinese or foreign firms from selling them dual-use goods; two of the ten, MP Materials and USA Rare Earth, are the federally backed American firms furthest along in building a mine-to-magnet supply chain.
insights.speaker: The Conversation
insights.so_what: China deliberately targeting the two most advanced US rare-earth reshoring companies is a direct, targeted countermeasure aimed at slowing the specific firms best positioned to reduce US dependency — a critical single-name risk factor for investors in MP Materials and USA Rare Earth.
insights.locator: Two of them—MP Materials and USA Rare Earth

insights.claim: The author, a former US Navy war-games adjudicator, interprets China's selection of MP Materials and USA Rare Earth for sanctions as a deliberate strategy to slow the specific companies best placed to reduce America's need for Chinese processing.
insights.speaker: The Conversation
insights.so_what: This is the article's core strategic read: China is playing a targeted, leverage-preserving game rather than blanket retaliation, a useful analytical frame for anticipating future Chinese export-control targeting decisions.
insights.quote: China picked MP Materials and USA Rare Earth because they are best placed to reduce America’s need for Chinese processing
insights.locator: Beijing said its move was a response

themes.theme: US rebuilding efforts and their limits

insights.claim: The US Government Accountability Office estimated in 2010 that rebuilding a full domestic rare earth supply chain (mining, separation, magnet manufacturing) could take as long as 15 years; rebuilding has been slow in practice partly because China runs its plants with thousands of experienced engineers versus far fewer US experts, and China banned exports of separation technology itself in December 2023.
insights.speaker: The Conversation
insights.so_what: A 15-year reshoring timeline estimate, combined with China's technology export ban, implies US rare earth self-sufficiency is a multi-decade structural project, not a near-term fix, relevant to any investment thesis premised on fast US supply-chain diversification.
insights.locator: The US Government Accountability Office cited estimates in 2010

insights.claim: The US government has committed more than $7 billion since April 2025 to rebuild domestic rare earth production capacity, including the Pentagon buying $400 million of preferred stock in MP Materials in 2025 (giving it 15 percent ownership) and the Commerce Department signing a 2026 letter of intent to give USA Rare Earth $277 million in direct funding plus a $1.3 billion loan for Texas and Oklahoma facilities.
insights.speaker: The Conversation
insights.so_what: Quantifies specific US government financial commitments and equity stakes (Pentagon's 15% of MP Materials; $1.58B combined support for USA Rare Earth) that directly affect these companies' balance sheets and government-backed downside protection, key facts for evaluating them as investments.
insights.locator: The US government has committed more than $7 billion

insights.claim: MP Materials expects its next magnet plant to begin testing equipment in 2028.
insights.speaker: The Conversation
insights.so_what: Gives a concrete near-term milestone (2028 equipment testing) for tracking MP Materials' progress toward actual magnet production capacity.
insights.locator: MP Materials expects its next magnet plant

insights.claim: Ford had to idle its Chicago assembly plant for a week in May 2025 due to a shortage of magnets critical to speakers and electrical motors, caused by China's export rules; Ford CEO Jim Farley described the company's magnet supply as 'day to day' since Ford had no alternate source, and production only resumed after Beijing granted approval.
insights.speaker: The Conversation
insights.so_what: A concrete, realized example of a major US automaker's production being halted by Chinese rare earth export controls demonstrates the real-world operational risk to manufacturers with no alternate rare earth magnet sourcing.
insights.locator: Automaker Ford saw how the export controls can affect a company

insights.claim: The article frames the US as facing three strategic paths: continuing to rely on cheaper, faster Chinese processing while remaining exposed to Beijing's restrictions; rebuilding a full domestic supply chain at high cost and with acidic/radioactive waste byproducts; or building a supply chain with allies such as Australia or Japan, which lowers unilateral cutoff risk but is still constrained by China's technology-use restrictions.
insights.speaker: The Conversation
insights.so_what: Provides a clean three-path decision framework (status quo dependency vs. full domestic build vs. allied diversification) useful for evaluating national rare-earth policy and identifying which companies/countries benefit under each scenario.
insights.locator: For the US, leaving processing in China is the fastest

insights.claim: Japan has already pursued the allied-diversification strategy with some success in reducing its rare earth dependency on China, though the suspended Chinese export rules still affect any use of Chinese rare earth technology abroad.
insights.speaker: The Conversation
insights.so_what: Japan serves as a real-world precedent/case study for allied rare-earth diversification strategies that the US or EU could emulate, though not a fully insulated solution given China's technology-use restrictions.
insights.locator: Japan has run this play with some success

insights.claim: President Xi's September 24, 2026 meeting with Trump may help determine the status of the November 10 export control restrictions, though the author notes the larger conflict over rare earth leverage will continue regardless of the meeting's outcome.
insights.speaker: The Conversation
insights.so_what: Flags a specific near-term diplomatic catalyst (September 24, 2026 Xi-Trump meeting, the article's own publication date) that investors in rare-earth-exposed sectors should watch for signals on whether the November 10 truce will be extended.
insights.quote: the larger conflict over leverage will continue
insights.locator: President Xi’s Sept. 24, 2026, meeting with Trump
